To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) alcohol dependence may be a complex genetic disease, (2) alcohol may alter neuronal functions through induction of novel genes, (3) the alcohol‐responsive genes are involved in the regulation of neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity, and (4) these alcohol‐responsive gene profiles are unique to alcoholism and may be used as biomarkers for the diagnosis of this disease.

(i) the human genome contains a number of alcohol‐responsive genes; (ii) the expression of alcohol‐responsive gene products is altered in the alcoholic brain; (iii) alcohol‐responsive genes are differentially expressed in the alcoholic brain, depending on the region of the brain; (iv) the induction of alcohol‐responsive proteins is associated with the development of tolerance and/or dependence on alcohol; (v) alcohol‐responsive proteins have a wide range in function; (vi) the alcohol‐

the human alcoholic brain has altered gene expression, and that the alcohol‐responsive genes identified to date are likely involved in the neuroadaptation of the alcoholic brain and the development of alcohol dependence.
